issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s defined right to receive a share of income from a wakf estate is an asset assessable to wealth tax, including where the share is treated as maintenance.
material_facts: The wakf deed entitled each beneficiary to a specified fraction of the estate’s net income, payable in monthly instalments during the beneficiary’s lifetime.
The beneficiaries were assessed to wealth tax on the capitalised value of their interests.
The court was not satisfied that the income shares were intended merely for maintenance and support, but held that the right would be an asset even if it were so intended.
issues.conclusion: The beneficiaries’ rights to receive their specified shares of income were assets assessable to wealth tax.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(e) and 2(m) of the Wealth Tax Act define assets and net wealth comprehensively, and section 3 charges wealth tax on net wealth; sections 4 and 5 address inclusion and exemption. “Property” has a wide meaning encompassing every interest a person can hold or enjoy. The court approved Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bombay City v. Purshottam N. Amersey and relied on Vidya Varuthi v. Balusami Ayyar and Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Shri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt. The court also considered the distinction between a life interest and income reserved for maintenance discussed in Abdul Karim Adenwalla v. Rahimabai, and the contention concerning non-transferability under section 6(dd) of the Transfer of Property Act.

predicates.wealth_tax_assessment: The proceeding assesses a person’s net wealth to wealth tax.
predicates.beneficiary_has_defined_income_share: A person is entitled under an arrangement to receive a defined share of income from an estate.
predicates.interest_is_not_limited_to_a_short_perio: The person’s interest is not confined to a period of six years or less.

issues.definition: When a wealth tax assessment concerns a person entitled to a defined share of estate income for more than a short period, the share right is assessable as an asset.

issues.legal_issue: The open-market valuation of an asset for wealth tax purposes is based on a hypothetical sale, not on proof of an actual sale or an actual market.
material_facts: The wealth tax assessment required valuation of the beneficiaries’ rights to receive shares of the wakf estate’s net income.
The beneficiaries argued that the rights could not be valued because they could not be sold in an actual open market.
issues.conclusion: The asset must be valued on the assumption that an open market exists and the asset can be sold there; an actual sale or actual market need not be established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(1) of the Wealth Tax Act requires the value of a non-cash asset to be estimated at the price it would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date. The court approved the approach in Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bombay City v. Purshottam N. Amersey and referred to Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Crossman in considering the hypothetical-market method.

predicates.wealth_tax_valuation_proceeding: The proceeding requires an asset to be valued for a wealth tax assessment.
predicates.non_cash_asset_requires_valuation: The asset being valued is not cash.

issues.definition: In a wealth tax valuation proceeding, a non-cash asset is valued on the assumed basis that it could be sold in an open market, whether or not an actual market or sale exists.

issues.legal_issue: A right to receive a defined share of estate income is not excluded from assets merely because it is argued to be a non-commutable annuity.
material_facts: The beneficiaries had rights under a wakf deed to receive defined shares of the net income in monthly instalments.
They argued that the rights were annuities whose terms or governing law precluded commutation into a lump sum.
The court rejected the argument that the word “annuity” should be given its popular or dictionary meaning rather than its judicially interpreted legal meaning.
issues.conclusion: The non-commutable-annuity exception did not exclude the beneficiaries’ income-share rights from assets assessable to wealth tax.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(e)(iv) of the Wealth Tax Act excludes a right to an annuity only where its terms and conditions preclude commutation of any portion into a lump sum. Where legislation uses a legal term that has received judicial interpretation, it is taken to use the term in that judicially interpreted sense, rather than merely its popular or dictionary meaning.

predicates.wealth_tax_assessment: The proceeding assesses a person’s net wealth to wealth tax.
predicates.beneficiary_has_defined_income_share: A person is entitled under an arrangement to receive a defined share of income from an estate.
predicates.non_commutable_annuity_exclusion_is_clai: The person claims that the income right is excluded because it cannot be converted into a lump sum.

issues.definition: If a person claims the non-commutable-annuity exclusion for a defined estate-income share in a wealth tax assessment, the income-share right is not excluded on that basis.
